title: Function declarations, prototypes and header declarations
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C language rules.
Trace the example and explain data flow.
Identify common errors and boundary conditions.
Apply the concept in a small tested program.

understand.concept: A function declaration introduces its name and type before use. A prototype specifies parameter types and return type, allowing the compiler to check calls. Header files commonly contain declarations shared between source files; definitions normally live in one implementation file.
understand.whyItMatters: Consistent declarations reduce mismatched calls and make multi-file programs easier to maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat a function or pointer operation as an explicit contract between caller and callee.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for types, object lifetime, scope and linkage.

explain.narrative:
A function declaration introduces its name and type before use. A prototype specifies parameter types and return type, allowing the compiler to check calls. Header files commonly contain declarations shared between source files; definitions normally live in one implementation file.

When applying this concept, check declared types, preconditions, object lifetime and all control-flow paths. Compile with warnings enabled and test both typical and boundary inputs.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The header declares add so main.c can compile a checked call. math_ops.c supplies the one function definition. Both translation units must agree on the function type.

practise.guidedTask: Explain why the declaration is needed before main calls add.
practise.independentTask: Split a small program into a header, implementation source and caller. Compile and link all source files together.
hints: Use include guards or #pragma once according to project policy to avoid repeated header inclusion.
Do not place ordinary external function definitions in headers included by multiple translation units.
